source_refs.note: A. Breaking of Covalent Bonds: a main subheading of 19.7 Understanding Organic Reactions, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 47-47.

blocks.text: There are two ways in which covalent bonds can break:
Homolytic fission occurs when the breaking bond is nonpolar. In this type of fission, the two shared electrons in the bond are distributed equally between the two atoms.

blocks.alt: Two homolysis equations. Cl-Cl gives Cl with a dot plus Cl with a dot; H3C-H gives CH3 with a dot plus H with a dot. In each, two single-barbed curved arrows start at the middle of the bond and go one to each atom.
blocks.caption: Homolytic fission of Cl-Cl and H3C-H (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: The dot (.) beside each atom indicates the unpaired electron that the atom has gained from the shared pair in the bond.
“These atoms or groups of atoms with unpaired electrons are called free radicals.”
highlight: “These atoms or groups of atoms with unpaired electrons are called free radicals.”

blocks.text: Free radicals are formed when a nonpolar bond is broken. These free radicals are the reaction intermediates and are highly reactive because of the tendency of their unpaired electrons to be paired.

In this type of fission, the two shared electrons in the bond are distributed unequally between the two atoms. One of the atoms keeps both electrons, and it acquires a negative charge. The other atom is deficient in one electron and, thus, acquires a positive charge.
Heterolytic fission occurs when the breaking bond is polar.
A species which contains a carbon atom with a positive charge is known as carbocation:
Carbocation is formed when carbon is bonded to a heteroatom whose electronegativity is more than carbon e.g; O, N, S, P etc.
Carbanion is formed when carbon is bonded to a heteroatom (metal) whose electronegativity is lesser than carbon e.g. Li, Mg, Cd etc.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Phosphorus (electronegativity 2.2) is less electronegative than carbon (2.5), so P does not belong in this list; sulphur (2.6) is about as electronegative as carbon. The atoms meant are those such as O, N and the halogens (e.g. Cl, as in the example below).

blocks.alt: (CH3)3C-Cl drawn with three CH3 groups on the central carbon; the carbon is marked +delta and Cl -delta, and a curved arrow runs from the C-Cl bond to Cl. The arrow leads to (CH3)3C+ (the central carbon with a + charge) plus Cl-.
blocks.caption: Formation of a carbocation from (CH3)3C-Cl (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).
